subject: Vocabulary
topic: Commonly Confused Words — Precise Usage and Distinctions (W12 B1)

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The cold weather ___ his performance significantly.' (affect / effect)
questions.explanation: B is correct. AFFECT (verb) = to have an impact on; to influence. EFFECT (noun) = the result or outcome. Here the blank requires a verb (subject 'weather' + ___ + object 'his performance') → 'affect' (verb). Note: 'affected' = past tense of affect; since the sentence is in Simple Present context (habitual), 'affects' would also be correct. Among the options, 'affect' (base form) fits a general statement. Trap: 'effect' = noun (wrong part of speech here); 'effects' = plural noun or rarely a verb meaning 'to bring about' (not the intended sense).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The school ___ announced new rules for examinations.' (principal / principle)
questions.explanation: C is correct. PRINCIPAL (noun) = the head of a school or college; (adjective) = most important/primary. PRINCIPLE (noun) = a fundamental truth, rule or moral standard. Here the blank is the head of a school → 'principal'. Memory trick: the principAL is your pAL (friend). PRINCIPLe has a final -le like ruLE (both refer to rules/standards). Trap: 'principle' = a rule, not a person; 'principled' = an adjective meaning 'having strong moral principles'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'She bought some ___ from the shop — pens, notebooks and envelopes.' (stationary / stationery)
questions.explanation: B is correct. STATIONERY (noun, -ery ending) = writing materials (pens, paper, notebooks, envelopes). STATIONARY (adjective, -ary ending) = not moving; fixed in one place. The context (pens, notebooks, envelopes) confirms 'stationery'. Memory trick: stationERY = lettERY (stationery relates to letters/writing). StationARY = stAY (staying in one place). Trap: 'stationary' = adjective (cannot describe a shop purchase of pens and notebooks).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'Her scarf ___ her dress perfectly — both were red and gold.' (complemented / complimented)
questions.explanation: B is correct. COMPLEMENT (verb) = to go well with or complete something; to make whole or perfect. COMPLIMENT (verb) = to express admiration or praise. Here the scarf matches and completes the dress visually → 'complemented'. Memory trick: complEment = complEte (both suggest completion/fitting together); complIment = polIte (both involve being polite/giving praise). Trap: 'complimented' = praised with words (a scarf cannot verbally praise a dress).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'After moving to a new country, she had to ___ to a different lifestyle.' (adapt / adopt)
questions.explanation: C is correct. ADAPT = to change or adjust oneself to suit new conditions; to modify for a new purpose. ADOPT = to take something (a child, an idea, a practice) as one's own; to formally take up. Here she must change herself to suit the new lifestyle → 'adapt'. If she were choosing and taking on a new lifestyle: 'She adopted a different lifestyle' (also possible but changes meaning slightly — 'adapt to' suggests adjusting, 'adopt' suggests choosing). Context: 'adapt TO a different lifestyle' uses the preposition 'to' which confirms 'adapt'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The earthquake was ___, but the dam collapse was ___ — we expected the dam to fail any day.' (eminent / imminent)
questions.explanation: D is correct. IMMINENT = about to happen very soon; impending. EMINENT = famous and respected, especially in a particular field. In context: the earthquake was unexpected (so it was 'imminent' in the sense of happening suddenly) — wait, actually the earthquake would also be 'imminent' if expected. Re-reading: 'we expected the dam to fail any day' = the dam collapse was imminent. And if the earthquake was 'surprising' the sentence would say 'unexpected'. Since both blanks describe events that were 'about to happen' (earthquake on that day, dam any day): both should be 'imminent'. D is correct: both = imminent. Trap: confusing eminent (famous) with imminent (impending) — classic SSC pair.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'The interrogators tried to ___ a confession from the suspect.' (elicit / illicit)
questions.explanation: B is correct. ELICIT (verb) = to draw out or evoke a response, reaction or information. ILLICIT (adjective) = not permitted by law or custom; illegal or forbidden. 'Tried to ___ a confession' = tried to draw out/evoke a confession → 'elicit'. Trap: 'illicit' is an adjective (cannot fill a verb blank); 'illicit' also sounds similar to 'elicit' — classic SSC confusable pair. 'Solicit' = to ask for or try to obtain, which is also possible here, but 'elicit' specifically means to draw out hidden information.

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'She has a natural ___ for languages, picking up new ones effortlessly.' (flair / flare)
questions.explanation: B is correct. FLAIR (noun) = a natural talent, ability or aptitude; a stylish quality. FLARE (noun/verb) = a sudden bright flame or light; to burn suddenly. 'Natural ___ for languages' = natural talent → 'flair'. Examples: 'She has a flair for cooking'; 'The rocket flare lit up the sky.' Trap: 'flare' = light/flame (completely wrong in context of language ability). The two words differ only in vowel but have completely unrelated meanings.

questions.stem: Choose the correct usage: 'The data ___ that patients recover faster with early treatment. Doctors ___ that early treatment helps from the data.' (imply / infer)
questions.explanation: A is correct. IMPLY (verb) = to suggest or indicate something indirectly (the WRITER or SPEAKER implies — the source gives the hint). INFER (verb) = to reach a conclusion from evidence (the READER or LISTENER infers — the interpreter draws the conclusion). 'The data IMPLIES that...' = data (source) suggests. 'Doctors INFER that... from the data' = doctors (observers) draw a conclusion from the data. Key memory: the Speaker/Source IMplies → the Listener INfers (I Make → I Note). Trap: confusing direction — many students say 'the data infers' (wrong: data cannot reason).

questions.stem: Choose the correct word: 'After the long flight, she just wanted to ___ down and rest.' (lie / lay)
questions.explanation: D is correct. LIE (intransitive) = to recline, rest horizontally; does NOT take an object. LAY (transitive) = to put/place something down; ALWAYS takes an object (lay the book, lay the table). Here: 'she wanted to ___ down' = she wanted to recline/rest → 'lie' (intransitive: no object follows). Trap: LAY seems correct to many speakers ('she lay down' is actually the PAST TENSE of 'lie'). Confusion: Lie (lie-lay-lain); Lay (lay-laid-laid). 'She lay down' = past of 'lie'; 'She laid the book down' = past of 'lay'. The blank is infinitive: 'to lie down' ✓.
